subject: MGMT160
title: Leading: Leadership, Motivation, Teams, Communication and Conflict

questions.stem: Describe leadership as the chapter defines it.
options: The ability to influence people to achieve goals
The right to give orders because of your position
Being the most experienced person in the team
Planning the schedules and budgets
questions.why: People follow leaders; they only obey bosses. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Differentiate what managers focus on from what leaders focus on.
options: Managers run the machine (planning, organising, controlling); leaders make people want to run it (inspiring, motivating, influencing)
Managers inspire and motivate the team day to day; leaders plan the budgets and control the results from a distance, usually from head office
Managers are born with the ability to organise; leaders are made through training in communication and public speaking
Managers lead small teams on the frontline; leaders lead whole departments or companies from the top of the chart
questions.why: Two skill sets, not two job titles — good managers need both. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Identify the three classic leadership styles.
options: Autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire
Strict, friendly, absent
Theory X, Theory Y, Theory Z
Transactional, transformational, situational
questions.why: Each style has a power and a price; the skill is knowing when to switch. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Describe the autocratic style and its price.
options: The manager decides alone — fast and clear, but ownership is low and ideas die unspoken
The manager decides with the team — slow, but the team is committed to the result once it is agreed
The manager steps back and lets the team decide — experts thrive, but beginners drown without direction
The manager never decides, so nothing is finished on time
questions.why: Autocratic fits emergencies, new staff and safety. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Explain why 'my door is always open' can go with 'our manager never listens'.
options: An open door is passive — real listening is active: the manager goes to people, asks, and visibly acts
Employees are usually wrong about their manager, because they only remember the times they were refused
Open doors are a security and confidentiality risk, so staff avoid using them for anything important
Listening is not part of a manager's job; the manager's job is to decide, and employees resent that
questions.why: An open door makes listening the employee's risk and effort. See the answer to question 3 in §6.2.

questions.stem: Identify the five levels of Maslow's hierarchy from the bottom up.
options: Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation
Self-actualisation, esteem, belonging, safety, physiological
Pay, security, promotion, recognition, meaning
Hygiene, safety, motivators, esteem, growth
questions.why: Needs come in layers; match the response to the need. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Describe motivation as the chapter defines it.
options: The willingness to work hard toward goals — the energy behind effort, direction and persistence
A fixed personality trait that some people are born with and others never develop, however hard they try
The salary and benefits an employee receives in return for the work they do
The manager's ability to give orders that employees carry out without question
questions.why: Motivation is not fixed: the same person performs differently under Manager A and Manager B. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Differentiate Herzberg's hygiene factors from motivators.
options: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction
Hygiene factors create excitement about the work; motivators remove the daily complaints
Both are about salary and bonuses
Hygiene factors are free to provide; motivators are expensive and need a budget
questions.why: Fair pay is like clean water: its absence poisons, its presence inspires nobody. Motivators — achievement, recognition, interesting work, growth — are mostly free. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Identify a hygiene factor.
options: Salary and working conditions
Recognition for a real achievement
Interesting work
Responsibility and growth
questions.why: Salary, conditions, policies, supervision quality and job security are hygiene factors. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Describe McGregor's Theory Y manager.
options: Assumes people want to do good work and can own responsibility, so builds ownership, clear goals and freedom in the how
Assumes people are lazy and must be watched at all times, so builds surveillance, tight rules, sign-in sheets and detailed daily reporting
Assumes people only work for money, so builds bonus schemes and commission for every task
Assumes managers should never trust anyone, so checks every piece of work before it leaves the team
questions.why: Your assumption becomes their reality: Theory X gets minimum effort, Theory Y gets ownership and early warnings. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Identify the four classic reasons teams fail.
options: Poor communication, unclear roles, conflict left to rot, poor leadership
Too much money, too much time, too many ideas, too many leaders and too few followers
Low salaries, bad offices, old computers, long working hours
Small size, young members, new products, strong competitors
questions.why: These four are what a team charter must answer in week 1. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four stages of the communication process.
options: Sender → message → receiver → feedback
Plan → organise → lead → control
Speak → repeat → write it down → confirm
Email → meeting → memo → report
questions.why: Every stage leaks; feedback — confirming what actually landed — is the stage most managers skip. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Describe active listening.
options: Full attention, listening to understand not to answer, asking questions and clarifying what you heard
Waiting silently until it is your turn to speak and then answering every point in order, without interrupting the other person
Nodding and making eye contact while composing your reply to what the person is saying
Leaving your door open so that anyone can come in and talk whenever they need to
questions.why: 'So if I heard you right, the problem is X?' See §6.7.

questions.stem: Differentiate task conflict from relationship conflict.
options: Task conflict is about ideas and is healthy; relationship conflict is about people and is the fire
Task conflict is about people and is the fire; relationship conflict is about ideas and is healthy
Both are always harmful, and the manager's job is to stop every disagreement quickly
Both are always healthy, because any argument shows that the team cares about its work
questions.why: Teams with zero disagreement usually have zero honesty. See §6.8.

questions.stem: Identify the four moves for managing a conflict, in order.
options: Stop the public fire → listen separately → reframe to the task → agree and follow up
Pick a winner → announce the decision → warn the loser → move on to the next task
Ignore the conflict → wait for it to cool → hope it is forgotten → avoid the subject
Listen to both together → ask the team to vote → publish the result → repeat if needed
questions.why: Never referee in front of the team; separately people tell the truth; a conflict without a follow-up date returns in a month. See §6.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the same team that performed badly under strict, silent Manager A and improved dramatically under supportive, clear Manager B. Determine what changed.
options: Only the manager — the people, pay and office were the same
The employees were replaced with more experienced staff hired by Manager B
The salaries were raised when Manager B arrived
The office was moved to a better location with more light and space
questions.why: The manager explains about 70% of engagement. See the answer to questions 1 and 2 in §6.1.

questions.stem: Select the leadership style for a hospital emergency room during an emergency, and after it.
options: Autocratic during the emergency; democratic in the debrief
Democratic during the emergency; autocratic in the debrief afterwards
Laissez-faire throughout, because emergency staff are highly trained experts
Autocratic throughout, because the ER is a safety-critical environment at all times
questions.why: Seconds matter, but the team must improve the protocol afterwards. See the table in §6.2.

questions.stem: Select the leadership style for a team of skilled, self-directed experts.
options: Laissez-faire — set direction and step back
Autocratic — decide alone, because experts argue too much to reach a decision
Democratic with daily votes on every technical question the team faces
None at all — experts do not need direction and resent any kind of manager
questions.why: Experts and creatives thrive with freedom; beginners would drown. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Determine the Maslow level of a well-paid star employee who is quietly unhappy because nobody ever says 'well done'.
options: Esteem — respect and recognition
Physiological — pay, food and rest
Safety — job security
Belonging — team and friendship
questions.why: The best-paid star may be starving at level 4. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who offers a 'growth opportunity' to an employee worried about paying rent. Determine the mistake.
options: Mismatching the response to the need — level 5 offered to a level 1–2 need
Offering too much money, when the employee really wanted a challenge and recognition
Ignoring the employee's talent and offering growth to the wrong person
Being too autocratic — the employee should have chosen the opportunity himself
questions.why: Someone worried about rent cannot be excited by growth; match the response to the need. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the Unhappy Team: salaries fine and paid on time, but 'nobody notices what we do' and 'every day is identical'. Determine the diagnosis.
options: A motivator problem — hygiene is fine; recognition, interesting work and ownership are missing
A hygiene problem — the salaries should be raised, because pay is what employees really notice
A safety problem — the team needs permanent contracts before it will feel motivated
Not a management problem — the team is simply bored, and boredom is part of every job
questions.why: Fixing hygiene removes complaints but does not create excitement; the missing pieces are motivators, which are mostly free. See §6.4 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select the zero-cost action that is a motivator, not a hygiene factor.
options: Trusting someone with a real responsibility and recognising a real achievement
Paying salaries on time and in full at the end of every month
Fixing the air conditioning so that the office is comfortable all summer
Giving everyone a company policy handbook so that the rules are clear to all of the staff
questions.why: Motivators — achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth — make people love Monday and are mostly free. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who installs surveillance and minute-policing, then finds the team gives minimum effort and stops thinking. Determine the chapter's explanation.
options: Theory X assumptions created the behaviour they expected — the resentment 'proved' she was right
Theory Y was applied too strongly, so the team took advantage of the freedom it was given
The employees were lazy from the start, and the surveillance simply revealed what was already there
Surveillance always improves performance, so the team must have been unusually difficult
questions.why: Your assumption becomes their reality. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Analyse why kindergarten children beat business-school students in the Marshmallow Challenge. Determine the lesson for teams.
options: Prototype early, share leadership, and put the goal on top from minute one
Children are physically stronger relative to the spaghetti, so their towers hold the weight
Business students had less spaghetti because they wasted some during the planning stage
Planning should take longer, because the students' towers failed from lack of preparation
questions.why: Business students plan and argue, build one perfect tower and put the marshmallow on in the final seconds — when it collapses. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the Friday 4:55 pm message 'prepare the client presentation, make it good, we need it soon' that produced 40 slides from Ahmed, 5 from Sara and no pricing section. Identify the barriers.
options: Undefined words ('soon', 'good'), no roles assigned, wrong channel and time, no feedback loop
The team was lazy and did not take the message seriously because it arrived late on a Friday afternoon
The channel was too formal, so the team did not feel able to ask what the manager meant
The message was too long, so Ahmed and Sara each read only the part that applied to them
questions.why: The rewrite says what exactly, for whom, by when, who owns which part, and asks for a reply. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Select the communication barrier in 'they obviously know what I mean'.
options: Assumptions
Poor listening by the team
Misunderstanding of a word
Wrong channel
questions.why: 'They obviously know what I mean' is the most expensive sentence in management. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Determine what a smart manager does when nobody disagrees in meetings but people complain afterwards.
options: Create safe channels — written input before meetings or going round the table — and never force public confrontation
Demand that everyone argues in public at every meeting, so that the team learns to disagree in the open and gets used to it
Cancel all meetings and make every decision alone, since the team will not speak anyway
Punish the people who complain afterwards, so that disagreement is raised in the meeting or not at all
questions.why: High respect for hierarchy makes public disagreement feel like humiliating the boss; harvest the insight privately. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Determine the right response when '9:00' means 8:55 to one colleague and 'the morning' to another.
options: Define the code explicitly — '9:00 means seated by 9:00' — a rule beats a resentment
Fire the late colleague, because punctuality is a basic requirement of any job
Move all meetings to the afternoon, when both colleagues are more likely to be on time
Assume the late colleague is rude and stop inviting them to the morning meetings
questions.why: Look for the cultural code before you judge the person. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Select the manager's first move when Khalid and Mariam argue loudly in the open office about whose numbers are right.
options: Stop the public fire calmly: 'Let's pause this — my office at 2'
Decide on the spot who is right in front of everyone, so that the argument ends quickly
Ignore it and let them finish, because adults should be able to settle their own disputes
Send both home for the day, so that the rest of the team can work in peace
questions.why: Never referee in front of the team; public resolution humiliates the loser and teaches everyone to fight publicly. See §6.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a conflict that was 'resolved' in a meeting but returned a month later. Determine the missing move.
options: Agree and follow up — one written decision with a date to check it
Stop the public fire — the argument should have been stopped more firmly in the meeting
Listen separately — the two people should have been heard one at a time before the meeting
Reframe to the task — the conflict should have been turned into a question about the work
questions.why: A conflict without a follow-up date returns in a month. See move 4 in §6.8.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a boss and a leader.
options: People obey a boss because of the position; people follow a leader because of influence
A boss is paid more than a leader and has a bigger office and a longer job title
A leader always has a bigger team than a boss, because people ask to join a leader's team
There is no difference; the two words describe the same job from different points of view
questions.why: People follow leaders; they only obey bosses. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Describe why good managers need both management and leadership skills.
options: Running the machine and making people want to run it are two different skill sets
Leadership is only for top managers, and management is for everyone below them
Management is only for small teams, and leadership is for large organisations
One replaces the other, so a manager who learns to lead no longer needs to manage
questions.why: Two skill sets, not two job titles. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Describe the laissez-faire style and when it fits.
options: The manager sets direction and steps back; it fits experts and creatives but drowns beginners
The manager decides everything alone; it fits emergencies, new staff and safety-critical work
The manager votes on everything with the team; it fits new staff who need to feel involved
The manager is absent from the team; it fits nobody and is never the right choice
questions.why: Laissez-faire: experts thrive, beginners drown. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Describe the belonging level of Maslow's hierarchy.
options: The need for friendship, team and acceptance at work
The need for pay, rest and a comfortable working environment
The need for job security and a predictable future
The need for recognition, respect and a sense of achievement
questions.why: Level 3 is belonging — team and friendship. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Explain why the chapter says motivation is not fixed.
options: The same person performs differently under different managers
Motivation is decided at birth
Only pay changes motivation, and only for as long as the pay rise is remembered
Motivation never changes after the first job, because habits are formed early
questions.why: Manager A vs Manager B: same person, different performance. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Describe what happens when a manager fixes hygiene factors only.
options: Complaints stop but nobody gets excited about the work
Employees become highly motivated and start to suggest improvements
Employees leave immediately, because fixing hygiene shows the manager has nothing else to offer
Productivity doubles, because comfortable employees work twice as hard
questions.why: Hygiene removes dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Describe a team charter.
options: A short agreement in week 1 on roles, communication, how conflict is handled and who leads
A list of team members' salaries and the share of the bonus each will receive
A legal contract with the customer that sets out what the team will deliver and when
A legal contract with the customer that sets out what the team will deliver, by when, and at what price
questions.why: The charter answers the four reasons teams fail before they appear. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Explain the lesson of the Marshmallow Challenge.
options: Prototype early and test often instead of planning one perfect attempt
Plan for as long as possible before building, so that the first attempt is the right one
Let the most senior person decide the design, so that the team does not waste time arguing
Never use the marshmallow until the structure is complete and has been checked by everyone
questions.why: Children test early; business students collapse at the end. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Identify the role of leadership in the chapter's view of teams.
options: Shared, clear and chosen for the task — not just the loudest voice
Always the most senior person, because experience is what a team needs most
Nobody should lead the team
The customer leads, because the customer knows best what the team should deliver
questions.why: Poor leadership is one of the four reasons teams fail. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Describe the feedback stage of communication.
options: Confirming what the receiver actually understood
Sending the message a second time in a different channel so that it is not missed
Writing the message down so that there is a record of what was said
Choosing the channel that best fits the message and the receiver
questions.why: Feedback — confirming what landed — is the stage most managers skip. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Identify the most expensive sentence in management, according to the chapter.
options: 'They obviously know what I mean'
'Let's have a meeting about it'
'Send me an email with the details'
'Good job, keep it up'
questions.why: Assumptions are the most expensive barrier. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Describe the 'wrong channel' barrier.
options: Using a medium that does not fit the message, like a long instruction by text at 4:55 on Friday
Speaking too quietly in a noisy open-plan office, so that half of the message is lost before it arrives
Using too many words, so that the receiver stops reading before the important part
Writing in capital letters, which the receiver reads as shouting and ignores
questions.why: Channel and timing are barriers. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Describe what high respect for hierarchy does to public disagreement.
options: It makes disagreeing in public feel like humiliating the boss, so people stay silent
It makes people argue more loudly, because they want the boss to notice their loyalty
It has no effect on disagreement, because people who care about the work will always speak
It makes meetings shorter, because people agree quickly and get back to their desks
questions.why: Harvest the insight privately through safe channels. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Explain what a smart manager does about different cultural codes for time.
options: Defines the code explicitly so a rule replaces a resentment
Judges latecomers as rude and excludes them from the meetings they miss
Ignores the difference and hopes the team will settle on one meaning by itself
Moves all meetings online, where lateness is less visible and less embarrassing
questions.why: Look for the cultural code before judging the person. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Describe a safe channel for disagreement.
options: Written input before a meeting, or going round the table so everyone speaks
Shouting in the open office so that everyone can hear both sides of the argument
An anonymous complaint to HR only, so that nobody knows who disagreed
No channel at all — managers decide alone and the team is informed afterwards
questions.why: Safe channels harvest honest views without public confrontation. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Explain why zero disagreement in a team is a warning sign.
options: Teams with zero disagreement usually have zero honesty
It means the team is perfect and has reached the highest stage of development
It means the manager is strong and has earned the complete trust of the team
It means the work is easy and does not raise questions worth arguing about
questions.why: Task conflict about ideas is healthy. See §6.8.

questions.stem: Describe the 'reframe to the task' move.
options: Turn a fight between people back into a problem about the work
Give each person a new job so that they no longer have to work together
Blame both people equally so that neither feels they have won
Ask the team to vote on who is right so that the decision is shared
questions.why: Move 3: reframe the relationship conflict as a task question. See §6.8.

questions.stem: Classify a supervisor whose staff do exactly what the rules say and nothing more.
options: A boss who is obeyed, not a leader who is followed
A leader with strong influence whose team follows the rules out of respect
A laissez-faire leader who has given the team full freedom within the rules
A democratic leader whose team has agreed the rules and follows them exactly
questions.why: Obedience without extra effort is the mark of a boss. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's explanation when a team's output doubles after only the manager changed.
options: The manager's influence changed how people wanted to work
The team members secretly changed, because the new manager hired better people
Pay was doubled at the same time, and the new manager took the credit
The office moved to a better building, and the team was happier in the new space
questions.why: The manager explains most of engagement. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Select the action that shows leadership rather than management.
options: Explaining why the goal matters so the team wants to reach it
Writing the monthly budget and checking it against the forecast
Checking the schedule and adjusting the shifts for next week
Filing the reports on time so that head office has the numbers it needs
questions.why: Leading makes people want to run the machine. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Select the style for training a brand-new employee on a dangerous machine.
options: Autocratic — clear instructions, no debate during the task
Laissez-faire — let them explore the machine and learn from their own mistakes
Democratic — vote with the new employee on which steps to follow and in which order
No style — let the machine teach the employee, since experience is the best teacher
questions.why: Autocratic fits new staff and safety. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who uses the democratic style for a fire evacuation. Determine the problem.
options: Wrong style for the situation — emergencies need fast autocratic decisions
Democracy is always wrong, because managers are paid to decide and not to ask
The manager should have used laissez-faire and let each person find their own exit
Nothing is wrong
questions.why: Each style has a situation; knowing when to switch is the skill. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Determine the Maslow level of a new employee who fears the company will close.
options: Safety — job security
Esteem — respect and recognition
Self-actualisation — growth and meaning
Belonging — team and friendship
questions.why: Safety = security of the job. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Select the right response for an employee who feels left out of the team.
options: Include them in team work and social moments — belonging
Give them a bigger bonus
Offer a promotion title so that they feel respected by the team
Give them a private office so that they can concentrate on their work
questions.why: Match the response to the need: belonging. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Classify 'the office is too hot and the computers are slow'.
options: Hygiene factor complaints
Motivator complaints about the work itself
Theory Y assumptions about the staff
Self-actualisation needs that are not being met
questions.why: Working conditions are hygiene. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a team where nobody knows who is doing the report and two people wrote it. Determine the failure.
options: Unclear roles
Poor leadership
Conflict left to rot
Too much talk
questions.why: Unclear roles is one of the four classic team failures. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Select the first thing a new project team should do in week 1.
options: Agree a team charter: roles, communication, conflict and leadership
Build the final product immediately so that the team has something to show
Choose a team name and a logo first
Wait for the manager to assign roles and set the deadlines for each stage
questions.why: The charter answers the four failures before they appear. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a team that spent all its time planning the perfect solution and delivered nothing. Determine the lesson.
options: Prototype early and improve — the Marshmallow Challenge lesson
Plan even longer next time so that the solution is perfect before building starts
Hire a consultant to tell the team what the perfect solution should look like
Work alone, because teams waste time arguing about the plan
questions.why: Put the marshmallow on from minute one. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Select the message that passes the feedback stage.
options: 'Please send the pricing section by Tuesday noon — reply to confirm you have it'
'Make it good, we need it soon, and let me know if you have any questions at all'
'Make it good, we need it soon'
'Do the usual and send it when it is ready; I trust you to get the details right'
questions.why: Clear, specific, with a reply requested. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a message sent by text at 4:55 pm on Friday asking for a big presentation. Identify the main barrier.
options: Wrong channel and timing
Too much detail
Too polite
Correct channel, wrong person
questions.why: Channel and timing are barriers. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Determine the manager's move when one colleague treats 9:00 as 8:55 and another treats it as 'the morning'.
options: Define the code: '9:00 means seated by 9:00'
Fire the late one, because punctuality is a basic requirement of any job
Ignore it, because the difference is cultural and will sort itself out in time
Start meetings at 10 so that both colleagues are more likely to arrive on time
questions.why: A rule beats a resentment. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Select the best way to get honest views from a team that never disagrees in public.
options: Ask for written views before the meeting
Demand public debate so that the team learns to disagree in the open
Punish silence by recording who spoke and who did not in each meeting
Cancel meetings and decide alone, since the team will not speak anyway
questions.why: Safe channels harvest the insight. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Classify two designers arguing about which layout is better.
options: Task conflict — healthy
Relationship conflict — the fire
A communication barrier
Groupthink
questions.why: Conflict about ideas is healthy. See §6.8.

questions.stem: Classify two colleagues who refuse to speak to each other after a personal insult.
options: Relationship conflict — the fire
Task conflict — healthy disagreement about the work
Normal teamwork — colleagues often need time apart
A hygiene problem — the office is too crowded for the two of them
questions.why: Conflict about people is the fire. See §6.8.
